blocks.text: The word art comes from the Latin word artum meaning “a practical skill or craft”. Art can be found in all the subjects. Art is a way of self-expression so it is part of the spiritual human needs and is part of their identity.

“The astonishing color drawings in motion show us that an artistic genius for drawing has existed from man’s very beginning. But those beautiful drawings were not only a means of expression or communicating pleasant ideas but there were rather expressions
f religious ideas” Maria Montessori

The skills of drawing took two directions, to support the human stories and the other to reproduce with exactness the images that he humans were able to see. This later tendency of perfection was taken to such an extreme that in a point in the art history we can see pictures which almost resemble a photography of what’s being painted. With the introduction of photography the demand for realistic paintings decreased and art took again a new direction, more impressionistic or expressionistic. Art in relation with language Once human beings communicated through spoken language, they started to use language as a way not only to express direct thoughts but to embellish them, to give them the magic that stroke of the imagination. From the simple stories to myths of the Greeks and the philosophers looking for a meaning, language evolved not only as a mean of communication but almost a magical capacity of transmitting feelings, ideas and ideals. Art in relation with music, movement In the Children’s House walking on the line it is a group activity, it helps the children feel bounded. It is a group effort because they have to be mindful and control their movements always considering those who are before you and after you. For this kind of activity they need cohesion and enjoy moving together as a group with a rhythm.

For the older children in elementary, playing music together, dancing or singing are extremely attractive as this activities are group activities which appeal to the developmental requirements of the age. In the Children’s House they had the opportunity to work with the Montessori bells in Elementary they have the tone bars, musical instruments and the freedom to connect the music with movement through dancing or drama.
Art in relation with mathematics
Art is deeply connected to mathematics, using the power of sequences, fractions, powers, geometry, and measurement.

The harmony of art is sometimes brought by the mathematical series and proportions (E.g. Fibonacci series). It is enough to have a look at the patterns used by the artists from the pre-historic times until today in the modern architecture to see the tight connection art has with geometry and arithmetic.
Nature as inspiration for art

Nature served as inspiration for the humans from the beginnings until today. Nature made the human mind wander and try to solve all the enigmas that the nature presented to the human being. The humans used art to reproduce what impressed them and made them wonder. They used art to please the forces of nature or as a mean of communication (E.g. rain dances).
Preparation of the child in the Children’s House

In the Children’s House it starts a preparation of the hand, of the senses helping the child to be more aware of what surrounds him and develop precision in his movements. The practical life activities help the child to strengthen the wrist muscles and to develop a precise eye-hand coordination. Even through sometimes art as such it is limited in the Children’s House, this is not an obstacle for the children to produce art spontaneously.
Art in the Elementary

If the mind and the hand are prepared the children can start drawing by themselves. The role of the guide is to give the child presentations on techniques so that the child he can use to express his own vision of the world that surrounds him. The children should be encouraged to practice without constantly comparing their work with their peers. Art is a form of self-expression and therefore each art piece has its own unique identity.

The environment should have an art corner where there are no carpets, a place easy to clean after working, in order and very attractive. The children should have access to good quality supplies, even if in a more reduced quantity, giving the children an
pportunity to reproduce their ideas with exactness. Beautiful work in the classroom comes from a beautiful and orderly environment with clear presentations.
Elements in art
Line
Shape
Form
Colour
Value
Texture
Space
Perspective
Principles in art
Emphasis
Balance
Proportion
Contrast
Movement
Rhythm
Pattern
Variety and harmony

The art supplies in the classroom should include: water colors, acrylic paint, brushes, colored pencils, crayons, different kinds of paper, pastels and special paper for it, ink, charcoal and special pencils for sketching. Materials for handwork like knitting, embroidery, crochets, clay and plasticine. It might be helpful to also have a place where children can let their work dry and a place store it.

The children should receive presentations on technique, the correct use of the instruments. The goal is not to have a product but to experiment and improve – the work has to be ordered and show a learning process. The children have to learn to be observant, solve problems, learn about design, criticize their own work and find constructive points. The elements in art should be presented one at a time and be related with examples in art, nature and architecture. The presentation
f an element can be followed by a presentation of a technique. Once all the elements are presented, it is the time for the principles
to be presented and help the children understand how the elements are used in art.

“To confer the gift of drawing, we must create an eye that sees, a hand that obeys, a soul that feels and in this task the whole life must cooperate. In this sense life itself it is the only preparation for drawing” Maria Montessori – The Advanced Method Vol. 2

When we look around, art it is everywhere and connected with all the fields of knowledge. The human beings from all over the world always felt the need for artistic expression. Music and dance, were passed from generation to generation meanwhile the other forms
f art can be seen from the physical remains (E.g. paintings, pottery, sculptures, architecture, writings, etc).

We would like the child to feel that he has different means to express himself, we would like the child to feel free to explore and be creative. We would like the children understand why the artistic expression it is something that unites the human beings. Art not only that brings variety to our world, it also allows the different humans from different cultures to express themselves and preserve their culture and identity.
“If you hear a voice within you say ‘you cannot paint’, then by all means paint and that voice will be silenced” Vincent van Gogh

The guide can introduce the colour wheel to the children. The guide introduces the primary colours: red blue and yellow and the secondary colours: green, orange and purple. On the colour wheel we can see the complementary/contrast colours: blue-
range, red-green and purple-yellow.
The guide can introduce the colour wheel depending on the temperature of the colours. The wheel can be divided in cold colours and warm colours.

The next step would be to have a look at the colours in different pictures or paintings and identify them, not only by the name of the colours also as contrasting colours, the colour temperature and of the colours are primary or secondary.
Examples in works of art:
Cosmic Synchromy, Russel.
Water lilies, Monet 1916.
Composition A, Mondrian 1923. Primary colours with white and black that are the extremes of colours mixtures.
Bedroom Arles, Van Gogh 1888. Contrasting colours 2.
Turning Road, Andre Derain 1906. Warm colours and contrast.
Untitled, Ton Schulten 2000. Very easy to do with children with a quick result.
Examples in nature:
Examples in architecture:

The guide can interconnect this lesson with the work that the children have done in geometry. A review of the kinds of lines is helpful before venturing into identifying the lines in architecture, nature or art.

Line is one of the most important Elements of Art. Imagine creating a painting, sculpture or design without drawing lines to divide the paper or canvas into shapes and forms. Think about how important a role Line plays in the creation process. Lines can communicate an idea or express a feeling. They can appear static or active. Lines define objects. We will take a look at how artists use line expressively.
Line
Is the path of a moving point: horizontal, vertical, diagonal.
Is the mark left by a tool: brush, pencil, pen, etc.
Defines the position and direction of a design, image or form.
Types of line include vertical, horizontal, diagonal, contour or a combination of these.
They may be curved, straight, thick, thin, smooth, long, short and so forth.
Lines are used to create shape, pattern, texture, space, movement and optical illusion in design.
The use of lines allows artist to demonstrate delicacy or force.
Curves may take us slowly uphill, or turn sharply twisting our mind as they turn
A line can express various moods and feelings. “A line is a dot that went for a walk” Paul Klee
Examples in works of art:
Supermarket, Ben Shahn 1975. Basically straight lines but also curved lines.
In the Magic Mirror, Paul Klee 1934.
Untitled, (super chief), Martin Ramirez 1954
Animals out of lines, Picasso. Quite easy for children to do.
Strip song, J. Seeley 1981.
Puddle painting, Ian Davenport, 2011.
Examples in nature:
Examples in architecture:

The guide can show a few examples from architecture, art and nature and how the shape is present in different forms of art. When we talk about shape we think of two dimensions only. Examples in works of art:
Ctesiphone 1, Frank Stella 1968.
Pigs, Franz Marc.
Atlantis, Pesoa.
Broadway Boogie Woogie, Mondriaan 1942Supermarket, Ben Shahn 1975.
Examples in nature:
Examples in architecture:
The guide can show a few examples from architecture, art and nature and how the form is present in all of these. When we talk about form we think of the three dimensions. Examples in works of art:
David, Michelangelo Buonarotti 1501. Hands are out of proportion.
Venus of Willendorf, 30.000BC.
Bust of African woman, Charles Henri Joseph Cordier 1851.
Examples in nature:
Examples in architecture:
The guide can show a few examples from architecture, art and nature and how the texture is present in all of these. Examples in works of art:
Giorgio V del Regno. You can almost feel the fur and the velvet. Something has been done with the brush to bring that textures so real.
Ladies of Arles Memory of the Garden at Etten, Van Gogh 1888.
Self portrait of degenerate artisti, Oskar Kokoshka 1937.
Ad Parnassum, Paul Klee. 1932.
Examples in nature:
Examples in architecture:

The guide makes a relation between the value of colour and the third colour box where the children might have already experimented with the value of the colour by arranging the colour tablets. The guide can show a few examples from architecture, art and nature and how the value is present in all of these. Examples in works of art:
Springendes Pferd, 1913, Franz Marc 1913. Fading of colours.
The car, John Brack 1955. Mainly all is made out of brown.
St V Francis Kneeling, Francisco Zurbaran 1635-1639. Value has todo a lot with shadow.
Blue Nude, Picasso 1902.
II Ramonscello, Dante Gabriel Rossetti 1856. Warm and cold colours, contrast, shade, texture, value of colours.
Land des Vergangenen Jahres, Ton Shulten 1999.
Examples in nature:
Examples in architecture:

The guide can show a few examples from architecture, art and nature and how the space is present in all of these. The guide can introduce the concept of positive and negative space and the shapes that the light and the absence of light create. The guide can show examples. Examples in works of art:
Springendes Pferd, 1913, Franz Marc 1913. Fading of colours.
Christine’s world, Andrew Wyeth 1917.
The Basket of Apples, Cezanne.
La Combe III, Ellsworth Kell 1951.
The temptation of St Anthony, Salvador Dali 1946. Here we can talk of nonrealistic art, dreamy, fantastic.

Shigeo Fukuda 1975. Negative and positive spaces with white and black colours. Examples of chair and square, 2 zebras. You can ask children which one is more in the front or in the back. It is actually depending on what you focus on.
Examples in nature:
Examples in architecture:
The guide can show a few examples from architecture, art and nature and how the perspective is present in all of these. Examples in works of art:
Ten Shulten.
Parallelepiped vents 545, Ron Davis 1977.
Rue de Paris, Wet weather, Gustave Caillebotte 1877. 2 points de fuite.
Gezicht op Delft, Johannes Vermeer 1660-1661.
Le Grand Jatte, Georges Seurat 1884-86. Warm and cold colours, perspective, line, shape, texture.
Examples in nature:
Examples in architecture:
There are different ways to empathize something in art:
Through colour
Contrast
Shape
Size
Use of colour value
Use of lines
The guide can show a few examples from nature, photography, or architecture where emphasis is used.
Examples in works of art:
Curiosity, Jeff Jordan, 2013
Art of Living, Rene Magritte, 1967
Courtney Mook
The night watch, Rembrandt
Composition 8, Wassily Kandinsky, 2923
Examples in photography:
Examples in architecture:

When we speak about “balance” in art it means that the emphasis is equally distributed over the painting. Our eyes are not drawn to one point but move over the painting from one side to the other side finding balance. The guide can show a few examples from nature, photography, or architecture where balance is used. Examples in works of art:
Ghent Alterpiece, Jan van Eyck, 1432
The last supper, Leonardo da Vinci, 1495 – 1498
Balance, Manoj Maurya, 2014
The Car, John Brack, 1955
Water lilies, Claude Monet, 1916
The gleaners, Jean-Francois Millet, 1857
Dance at le Moulin de la Galette, Edouard Manet
Examples in photography:
Examples in architecture:

As we see pattern in the fur, feathers and scales of animals we can ding patterns in our surroundings and in the art. Pattern is often used as decoration; think of fabrics, carpets and wallpaper. The guide can show a few examples from nature, photography, or architecture where balance is used. Examples in art:
M. C. Escher
The kiss, Gustav Klimt, 1907 – 1908
Bullfighter, Ricardo Maya, 1910-1970
Daydream, Aphonse Mucha, 1897
Examples in photography:
Examples in architecture:

When we see a repeating pattern we can speak about rhythm. There are regular and irregular rhythms. The guide can show a few examples from nature, photography, or architecture where rhythm is used. Examples in art:
In a forest of dreams, Zuzanna Krol
Krishnakali Roy
Endless Rhythm, Robert Delaunay, 1934
High Sky, Bridget Riley, 1991
Squares with Concentric cocrcle. W. Kandinsky
Marilyn Monroe, Andy Warhol, 1962
Examples in photography:
Examples in architecture:

It is interesting how we can suggest “movement” on something that is actually standing still. It is interesting to ask the children to identify the movement in the pictures. The guide can show a few examples from nature, photography, or architecture where movement is used. Examples in art:
Starry night, Van Gogh
The great wave of Kanagawa, Hokusai
Dancers in the classroom, Edgar Degas, 1880
The dance, Henri Matisse, 1910
In the car, Roy Lichtenstein, 1963
Examples in photography:
Examples in architecture:
Proportion is something the artist can use to make it look realistic. When things are out of proportion it is a way to place emphasis
n something. Proportion also helps to create perspective in a painting; things closet to the observer are then bigger than things
there further away. The guide can show a few examples from nature, photography, or architecture where proportion is used. Examples in art:
Vitruvian Man, Leonardo da Vinci
Chirstina’s World,
Les Valeurs Personnelles, Rene Magritte
Elephants, Salvador Dali
Examples in nature:
Examples in architecture:
Contrast can be used in different ways:
Contrast in colour
Dark v.s light colours
Warm vs cold colours
Contrasting colours
Contrast in shape
Contrast in texture
Contrast in size
The guide can show a few examples from nature, photography, or architecture where contrast is used.
Examples in art:
Face, Liman
Landscape, Stephanie Maclean
Wheatfield with crows, van Gogh
Harmony, Loui Jover
Examples in photography:
Examples in architecture:

Variety and harmony go hand in hand and are very much dependent on the opinion of the observer. Harmony is related to balance, when the viewer’s eyes is taken over the piece of art with equally distributed emphasis. Variety makes an artwork interesting: little differences that keep you looking. The guide can show a few examples from nature, photography, or architecture where variety and harmony are used. Examples in art:
Waterliliees ,Monet
Nature’s Harmony, Mark Keathley
Lost love, Leonid Afremov, 2005
Examples in architecture:
Another principle that we could add is composition. Composition has to do with how the artist placed the components in his piece
f art.
Where did he put the emphasis?
Is there a balance?
Can we see harmony?
Are objects placed in the right proportion to create a perspective?
Is there a space created by the way the components are used?
Do we see a shape in the composition?
Do we see lines in the composition?
The elements and the principles in art can be introduced in lower elementary and revisited in upper elementary so that the children can explore in more depth.
